title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
claim: Implicit model-internal reasoning leaves transformations unchecked and errs; explicit executable world states ground each step in simulator feedback and answer correctly.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right, three shared stage columns, red vs blue
description: A two-row comparison under a header sentence: 'a left turn changes what is behind the observer.' A legend at top right marks hidden space (gray), executable space (light blue), observer (triangle) and object (orange square). Three shared column titles run across the top: Represent the scene, Apply the transformation, Derive the answer. The top row is red-orange, labeled 'Model reasoning, Model-internal'. A robot icon moves through gray panels, 'Implicit representation' and 'Unexecuted transformation' (with a red X) and 'Imagination'. It ends with 'IN FRONT' and a red cross. The bottom row is blue, labeled 'Agentic reasoning, Spatial Harness'. A robot writes an 'Executable world state' document, executes a turn in a grid 'Physics engine' with feedback arrows, reads the 'Feedback' grid, and ends with 'BEHIND' and a blue check mark. The color contrast draws the eye first.
caption: From model-internal reasoning to executable world states. Both approaches proceed from scene representation through spatial transformation to answer derivation. Top: a VLM implicitly represents the scene and imagines the requested turn, leaving the resulting spatial relation unchecked. Bottom: Spatial Harness constructs an explicit world state and executes the turn in a physics engine, grounding the answer in computed feedback. This makes both the estimated layout and the consequences of the transformation available for inspection. Execution enforces consistency with this state, whose accuracy still depends on the available language constraints and visual estimates.
abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness
